text: Publish a microarchitectural side-channel position statement: what isolation the capability model claims, which shared resources (glyph atlas, shared MemoryObjects, SMT siblings) are cross-domain channels, and which mitigations are on by default.
Provide the system CA trust store as a typed object with per-application pinning and enterprise-CA enrolment, consumed by native TLS and mirrored into the personalities' certificate stores.
Publish the threat model before capability, security and boot designs are fixed; every CAP/SEC/BOOT decision cites the threats it addresses.
Add a threat register (T-IDs) that CAP, SEC and BOOT decisions cite.
Accept the capability grant taxonomy decision (one-time, session, persistent, revocable-by-user) before the package capability-request schema.

lens: Legal, licensing and governance
text: Establish a security response process: SECURITY.md, coordinated-disclosure embargo policy, CNA application and linux-distros list participation once publicly distributed.
rationale: A kernel fork owns CVE response and needs embargoed access to upstream fixes.

lens: Legal, licensing and governance
text: Decide whether to run a bug bounty program and how it is funded.
rationale: A public beta benefits from external researchers but a bounty is a legal and financial commitment.

lens: Legal, licensing and governance
text: Assess EU Cyber Resilience Act obligations (open-source steward versus manufacturer status, vulnerability handling, SBOM, update duration) and plan compliance for 1.0.
rationale: A publicly distributed OS with digital elements falls under the Act's reporting and update duties.

lens: Legal, licensing and governance
text: Do not pursue formal security certifications (Common Criteria, FIPS 140) for 1.0.
rationale: Certification cost and process would divert effort from the stability contract without benefiting the target audience.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Track every unsafe block in native code with a required SAFETY comment, a CI-generated unsafe inventory per crate, and a trend line so unsafe surface area is a reviewed metric.
rationale: §51 requires unsafe authority to be minimised and isolated, which needs measurement to be enforceable.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Fuzz all userspace parsers of untrusted input (package manifests, environment.yaml, fonts, images, capability serialisation, personality PE/ELF loaders) with cargo-fuzz corpora maintained in the repository.
rationale: Parsers are the historical entry point for most desktop OS exploits.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Publish a written threat model naming adversaries (malicious native app, compromised component, compromised compatibility app, local unprivileged user, evil-maid with device off, evil-maid with device suspended, malicious DMA peripheral, network attacker, supply-chain attacker), protected assets, and trust boundaries, and require every CAP/SEC/BOOT ADR to cite which threats it addresses.
rationale: The baseline asserts 'no ambient authority' but never says what the system defends against, so 1.0 security claims cannot be evaluated or audited without it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Enable kernel lockdown (integrity or confidentiality mode) automatically when Secure Boot is active: no unsigned kexec, no raw physical memory access, no unsigned hibernation image, no debugfs writes.
rationale: Secure Boot without lockdown only protects the first boot stage and is trivially bypassed from a compromised root.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide whether TPM 2.0 is a hard hardware requirement for 1.0 or an optional enhancement, and define the degraded behaviour (passphrase-only unlock, no measured boot) on machines without one.
rationale: Measured boot, sealed disk keys and PCR-bound policy all depend on this and it must be reflected in the hardware compatibility database.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Expose the TPM to userspace only through a capability-gated TPM service; no ambient /dev/tpm0 or tpm2-tss access for applications.
rationale: A shared TPM device node lets any application exhaust, lock out or misuse platform keys.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Expose the TPM event log and PCR state locally through os inspect, and declare remote attestation (attestation server, enterprise enrolment) a non-goal for 1.0.
rationale: Local inspection satisfies §64's understandability goal while remote attestation would pull an enterprise trust infrastructure into a desktop 1.0.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the disk-encryption mechanism: reuse LUKS2/dm-crypt under the storage stack versus filesystem-native per-directory encryption versus both, respecting §57's rule against inventing new storage layers.
rationale: V1 developers daily-drive laptops with source code and credentials; encryption must be in place before any lost laptop is possible.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Seal the disk key to TPM PCR state with an optional PIN, and always generate an offline recovery key that the user must save (print, file to removable media) before installation completes; no cloud escrow by default.
rationale: PCR-bound unlock gives passwordless boot on healthy hardware, but firmware updates and motherboard replacement need a guaranteed recovery path.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Re-seal TPM-bound disk keys automatically before and after firmware updates and Secure Boot key changes so a PCR change never strands the user at the recovery-key prompt.
rationale: Firmware updates are the most common cause of TPM unlock failure on shipping OSes.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Support passphrase change and key-slot rotation without re-encrypting the volume, and cryptographic erase (key destruction) as the factory-reset primitive.
rationale: Users must be able to rotate credentials after a compromise and to hand over or dispose of hardware safely.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide whether disk keys are evicted from memory on suspend (requiring re-unlock on resume or suspend-then-hibernate) and whether hibernation is supported at all under lockdown, which requires an encrypted, authenticated hibernation image.
rationale: A suspended laptop with keys in RAM is the dominant realistic attack on encrypted laptops and the baseline lists suspend/resume as a V1 requirement.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: ADR: whether a user is a kernel-level identity (uid-like) or purely a userspace identity-service concept mapped to capability roots, and how the Linux personality's uid/gid expectations are derived from it.
rationale: The baseline never says what a 'user' is in a capability system, yet login, home data, secrets and compatibility all hinge on it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build an identity service holding local accounts with Argon2id-hashed credentials, exposed only through capability-gated typed interfaces (no readable shadow file) and pluggable authenticator interfaces for future methods.
rationale: Login at V1 needs somewhere to store and verify credentials, and the storage must not be ambient-readable like /etc/shadow-adjacent data has historically been.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Introduce a Session object linking user identity, seat, display and the session's capability root, with lock, unlock, idle, suspend-inhibit and end-of-session as typed interfaces replacing logind's D-Bus API for native software.
rationale: Lock screen, power management, per-session services and compatibility shims all need one authoritative session lifecycle.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a native login greeter integrated with the compositor, supporting password login at V1 and fingerprint and FIDO2/passkey login at V3.
rationale: V1 daily driving requires logging in, and later biometric and hardware-key methods are expected on modern laptops.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the multi-user scope for 1.0: number of local accounts, fast user switching, concurrent graphical sessions, and whether per-user home data is encrypted with per-user keys unlocked at login.
rationale: Each of these multiplies session, encryption and compositor complexity and must be scoped before the identity and storage designs are finalised.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Declare multi-seat, guest sessions, kiosk mode and enterprise directory login (LDAP/AD/Kerberos/SSO) non-goals for 1.0 while requiring the identity service's authenticator interface to remain pluggable.
rationale: These are enterprise and shared-machine features that would divert effort from the single-owner desktop the milestones describe.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a privilege-elevation Authorization service that grants scoped capabilities after re-authentication with an audit record, replacing sudo/polkit; native packages contain no setuid binaries.
rationale: Administrative actions (installing drivers, changing system settings) need an authority path that fits the capability model rather than reintroducing root.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define what 'administrator' versus 'standard user' means in capability terms, which operations require elevation, and that the first account created is an administrator.
rationale: Every settings panel and installer flow needs to know which actions elevate, and the roles must exist before the Settings app is built.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a native secrets service in which each application's secrets are capability-scoped objects encrypted under a per-user key unlocked at login, so no application can enumerate or read another application's secrets.
rationale: Today's Secret Service lets any app in the session read every stored password; the capability model should fix this and V1 developers need somewhere to keep tokens.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide an SSH agent and Git credential integration backed by the native secrets service, with optional TPM- or FIDO2-resident keys.
rationale: V1 self-hosting requires Git over SSH and developers will otherwise store keys in plain files.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Research whether the OS should act as a WebAuthn platform authenticator (passkey provider) backed by TPM and biometrics, and what browser integration that requires.
rationale: Passkeys are becoming the default login method on the web and a 1.0 desktop without a platform authenticator pushes users to third-party managers.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the taxonomy of user-mediated grants: which capabilities are granted implicitly by OS choosers (files, contacts), which require a prompt (camera, microphone, location, notifications, persistent background execution), and which are settings-only, with a documented rationale against prompt fatigue.
rationale: §9 assumes grants happen but never says how the user is asked, and prompt design decides whether the capability model is usable or ignored.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Do not expose stable hardware or installation identifiers (machine ID, TPM EK, disk serials, MAC addresses) to applications without a capability; provide per-application derived identifiers where needed.
rationale: Ambient device fingerprinting contradicts no-ambient-authority and is trivially available on Linux today via /etc/machine-id and sysfs.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Support hardware security keys (FIDO2 hmac-secret) as an additional disk-unlock and login factor.
rationale: Security-conscious enthusiasts targeted at public alpha expect hardware-key unlock and it exercises the pluggable authenticator interface.

lens: Desktop essentials the baseline omits
text: Location service exposing coarse (timezone, Wi-Fi geolocation) and precise location as separate capabilities with a shell indicator while in use.
rationale: Timezone detection, maps, and weather need it and it is one of the most sensitive ambient permissions on existing desktops.

lens: Release engineering and operations
text: Publish a security policy with a reporting contact, encrypted channel, disclosure timeline, embargo rules and CNA registration for the project's own CVEs.
rationale: Public alpha invites vulnerability reports and researchers need a defined channel.

lens: Release engineering and operations
text: Commission an independent security audit of the capability system, native ABI and update pipeline before 1.0.
rationale: A security model that has only been reviewed by its authors cannot be called stable.

lens: Migration, adoption and interoperability
text: Active Directory domain join, Group Policy and enterprise fleet management are explicitly out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Stating the nongoal stops enterprise-shaped requirements from distorting the identity and settings model before the desktop is stable.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the disk encryption layer (dm-crypt/LUKS block level, fscrypt file level, or filesystem-native) and its interaction with snapshots and content-addressed dedup.
rationale: Encryption choice constrains filesystem choice and per-user data isolation, and must precede the storage ADR.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Write a threat model document enumerating attacker classes (malicious app, compromised component, malicious peripheral, evil maid, remote) before capability, personality and storage security designs are frozen.
rationale: Security decisions in every workstream need a shared reference for what they are defending against.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the identity and login model (local accounts, hardware-backed keys, session capability roots) and how a login session becomes the root capability holder.
rationale: The capability tree must have a defined root or the desktop shell ends up with ambient authority.

text: Study secure enclaves (SGX/SEV-style) as a possible home for components requiring hardware confidentiality.
A native application must not automatically receive filesystem access; add a conformance test.
A native application must not automatically receive home directory access.
A native application must not automatically receive camera access.
A native application must not automatically be able to enumerate other processes or components.
A native application must not automatically receive device access.
A native application must not automatically receive location access.
A native application must not automatically receive other applications' data.
ADR: which authority sources exist (manifest request, launcher policy, user chooser, permissions UI, delegation from another component) and their precedence.
ImageDecoder must have no network access; verify with an integration test.
ImageDecoder must have no arbitrary filesystem access; verify with an integration test.
ImageDecoder must have no microphone access.
ImageDecoder must have no process enumeration.
An exploit must compromise only the smallest useful unit of software; the threat model must evaluate blast radius per component.
MemoryObject supports the encrypted property.
Resolve semantics of encrypted MemoryObjects: key ownership, who can map plaintext, and interaction with hardware memory encryption.
Define which intents (Realtime, LowLatency) require a capability to request and how the system prevents an unprivileged Component from starving others.
Tracing must be security-aware: reading traces of another Component requires a capability, and trace payloads must not leak message contents without explicit authority.
User-space drivers must require IOMMU protection for DMA so a compromised driver cannot read arbitrary physical memory.
Decide the verified-once trust mechanism for cached verification (dm-verity style block verification, signed content-store index, or per-launch hash of a small manifest).
No application receives unrestricted screen capture; capture is only possible through an explicit screen-share capability.
Remote use of interfaces must still honour capabilities.
Remote use of interfaces must honour identity of both endpoints.
Remote use of interfaces must be encrypted.
Remote use of interfaces must be subject to explicit user policy; no silent remote access.
AI actions must be permissioned (each requires a held capability).
AI capability grants must be scoped (to a project, a file, a time window), not blanket.
Provide a consent/permissions UI for granting capabilities to an assistant per request (§63 permissions UI).
Resolve whether an AI assistant is a distinct security principal from the user for audit and revocation purposes.
Present compatibility-application capability grants in the same permissions UI as native applications.
Decide the default capability profile for compatibility applications (how much filesystem/network authority a Linux or Windows app gets without prompting) (ADR).
'Use Rust' is not the complete memory-safety strategy; defence in depth is mandatory.
Language safety layer: Rust with unsafe minimised across kernel and platform code.
Hardware enforcement layer where available (§8); design hooks now, enable on capable hardware later.
Unsafe authority must be minimised and isolated into audited components.
Write the platform threat model document covering each safety layer and its assumed adversary.
Retain and enable Linux kernel hardening features (KASLR, CFI, stack protector, SMEP/SMAP, IBT/CET) in the fork.
Evaluate x86-64 hardware enforcement mechanisms (MPK/PKU, CET shadow stacks, LAM) for isolating unsafe code within components.
Study Android permissions, Binder IPC, app sandboxing and A/B system updates.
Permissions UI to view, grant and revoke application capabilities.
Inspection authority is itself a capability (Capability<Inspect> scoped to a ResourceDomain or component subtree) so introspection is not ambient.
Principle 3: security comes from authority design, not deny lists; blocklist-based sandboxing may not be the primary security mechanism.
